Joint distribution: First metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra) most common; also ankles, knees, elbows, wrists, fingers, and the ear helix. — Lower temperature in distal joints favors crystal precipitation; mechanical stress and reduced blood flow promote nucleation.

A 55-year-old obese man develops sudden onset of severe pain, redness and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

qs.q: A 60-year-old man presents with acute, severe pain, swelling, and erythema of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint aspiration reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. What is the fundamental metabolic trigger for crystal precipitation?
o: Excessive renal tubular reabsorption of filtered calcium
Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate within joint cartilage
Overproduction or underexcretion of purine catabolites
Enzymatic breakdown of synovial collagen by matrix proteins
Precipitation of cholesterol clefts within synovial fluid
qs.e: Gout is caused by hyperuricemia resulting from purine metabolism abnormalities, leading to monosodium urate crystal precipitation.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 55-year-old man presents with severe pain and swelling in his first metatarsophalangeal joint. Synovial fluid analysis reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. Which metabolic pathway leads to the accumulation of these crystals?
o: Overproduction or underexcretion of purine end-products.
Impaired lysosomal degradation of complex sphingolipids.
Defective pyrophosphate metabolism in cartilage matrix.
Abnormal deposition of amyloid fibrils in tissues.
Accelerated cholesterol ester precipitation in cells.
qs.e: Gout is caused by hyperuricemia resulting from purine metabolism breakdown, leading to monosodium urate crystal deposition.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 60-year-old man experiences excruciating pain, erythema, and swelling in the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Arthrocentesis reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. What initiated crystal formation?
o: Supersaturation of urate in synovial fluid
Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals
Precipitation of basic calcium apatite deposits
Aggregation of neutral lipid globules
Crystallization of cholesterol ester particles
qs.e: Gout occurs when monosodium urate crystals precipitate in joints due to hyperuricemia and supersaturation of synovial fluid.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Internal Medicine Exam - October 24, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 50-year-old man with chronic hyperuricemia experiences a sudden, exquisitely painful attack of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. What is the initial molecular event following MSU crystal phagocytosis by synovial macrophages?
o: Complement system depletion by crystals
Inhibition of xanthine oxidase activity
Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome
Urate crystal dissolution by neutrophils
qs.e: When MSU crystals are phagocytosed by macrophages, they activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to the release of IL-1β and subsequent intense neutrophilic inflammation. Xanthine oxidase is involved in purine catabolism and hyperuricemia, not the downstream inflammatory cascade.
qs.s: Infectious Arthritis: Bacterial, TB & Viral Joint Infections: MCQs

qs.q: A 54-year-old man presents with a severely painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint that developed overnight. Synovial fluid analysis reveals needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Which cellular process directly triggers the acute inflammatory response in this joint?
o: Phagocytosis of precipitated monosodium urate crystals by polymorphonuclear neutrophils
Autoimmune-mediated proliferation of synovial lining cells with immune complex deposition
Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals within the articular cartilage
Direct bacterial invasion of the synovial space following minor soft tissue trauma
qs.e: Acute gout flares are driven by neutrophils phagocytosing monosodium urate crystals, which triggers inflammasome activation and cytokine release. Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition causes pseudogout rather than classic acute gout.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with acute, severe pain, swelling, and erythema of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of his right foot that woke him up at night. What is this classic manifestation called?
o: Gonagra affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Tophi affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Chiragra affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Podagra affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint
qs.e: Podagra refers to inflammation of the MTP joint of the big toe, which is the most common site for acute gouty arthritis. Gonagra and chiragra refer to knee and finger joint inflammation, respectively.

qs.q: A 64-year-old man with a 15-year history of poorly controlled hyperuricemia presents with firm, painless, yellowish-white nodules over his left olecranon bursa and first metatarsophalangeal joints. What is the underlying histological composition of these lesions?
o: Aggregates of monosodium urate crystals surrounded by chronic inflammatory cells
Necrotic adipocytes enclosed within a thick fibrous connective tissue capsule
Dystrophic calcium phosphate deposits within damaged tendon insertions
Proliferating synovial lining cells mixed with acute neutrophilic infiltrate
qs.e: Tophi consist of dense aggregates of monosodium urate crystals surrounded by macrophages, lymphocytes, and foreign-body giant cells. They are distinct from lipomas, purulent abscesses, or pure calcium deposits.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a hot, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint. Arthrocentesis is attempted twice by different clinicians, but insufficient synovial fluid is obtained for crystal analysis. Which diagnostic imaging modality is best indicated next?
o: Ultrasound of the joint
Magnetic resonance imaging
Contrast-enhanced CT scan
Technetium bone scintigraphy
qs.e: Ultrasound is the preferred non-invasive imaging modality to evaluate for the double-contour sign and tophi when joint fluid cannot be obtained. Scintigraphy and MRI lack the specific spatial resolution required for crystal identification.

ai.title: Gout of the First Metatarsophalangeal Joint (Podagra)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Podagra is acute gout affecting the big toe joint, common in low‑resource settings where diet, dehydration and infections raise uric acid. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and joint aspiration; management targets urate reduction and inflammation.

sections.p: Podagra is an acute mono‑articular arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition.
b: Clinical triad: sudden severe pain, swelling, erythema of the big toe
Joint aspiration showing negatively birefringent needle‑shaped crystals confirms diagnosis

t.b: Does the joint contain urate crystals? Positive crystals confirm gout; absence suggests other arthritis
Is hyperuricemia present? Elevated >7 mg/dL supports gout but normal level does not exclude it
Are there erosions with overhanging edges? Chronic changes support gout; may be unavailable, rely on clinical picture

sections.p: Acute attacks are staged as mild, moderate or severe based on pain, swelling and functional limitation.
b: Mild: pain tolerable, able to walk with limp
Moderate: severe pain, unable to bear weight, marked swelling
Severe: excruciating pain, systemic fever, possible renal involvement

sections.p: Hyperuricemia results from overproduction or under‑excretion of uric acid; precipitating factors are common in East Africa.
b: Diet high in purines (red meat, organ meat, seafood)
Dehydration from hot climate or diarrhoea
Alcohol, especially local brews
Renal disease, diuretic use, hypertension
Infections (TB, HIV) and certain herbal remedies that impair renal urate clearance

sections.p: The patient reports a sudden onset (often at night) of intense throbbing pain in the big toe, with redness, swelling and warmth.
b: Pain peaks within 24 h, may be accompanied by fever
Joint is hot, tender, and the skin may appear shiny
Limited dorsiflexion of the toe

sections.p: In low‑resource settings prioritize bedside tools; laboratory tests are added when available.

t.b: Confirms crystal type; if unavailable, treat as gout based on classic presentation
Helps identify hyperuricemia; normal level does not rule out gout
Assesses need for dose adjustment of urate‑lowering drugs
Detects leukocytosis suggesting infection if joint is septic

sections.p: Recognise features that demand urgent referral.
b: Rapidly spreading erythema, fever, high white cell count → septic arthritis
Renal failure or uric acid nephrolithiasis
Tophi causing skin ulceration or nerve compression

sections.p: Treat the acute attack first, then address long‑term urate control.
b: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) if no renal contraindication – reduce inflammation quickly
Colchicine low‑dose regimen – useful when NSAIDs unavailable or contraindicated
Corticosteroid injection or oral prednisolone for severe attacks or renal disease
Allopurinol or febuxostat for chronic urate lowering – start after the acute flare resolves
Lifestyle: increase water intake, limit purine‑rich foods and alcohol, weight control

sections.p: Regular review of uric acid levels and adherence to urate‑lowering therapy prevents recurrences.
b: Check serum uric acid 4‑6 weeks after starting allopurinol; target <6 mg/dL
Educate on hydration and diet; monitor renal function annually
Assess for tophi development during clinic visits

sections.p: Other causes of acute mono‑arthritis of the toe.
b: Septic arthritis – usually more systemic signs, purulent aspirate
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) – positively birefringent rhomboid crystals
Traumatic sprain – history of injury, no crystals

sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or misleading findings.
b: Serum uric acid may be normal during an acute attack
Joint fluid may be paucicellular early, mimicking non‑infectious arthritis
Radiographs can be normal early; rely on clinical picture

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid spread of redness beyond the toe
Severe renal pain or decreased urine output

faq.q: Can gout occur with normal serum uric acid?
faq.a: Yes; uric acid can be normal during an acute flare, so crystal identification is decisive.

faq.q: Why avoid NSAIDs in renal disease?
faq.a: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin synthesis, risking acute kidney injury.

faq.q: When can colchicine be used safely?
faq.a: Low‑dose colchicine is safe in mild renal impairment; avoid high doses in severe renal failure.

exam: A 48‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden right big‑toe pain and swelling; what is the next best step? — Perform joint aspiration for crystal analysis before starting therapy.
How does podagra differ clinically from septic arthritis of the first MTP? — Gout shows intense pain with minimal systemic signs; septic arthritis has fever, leukocytosis, purulent fluid.
Why is colchicine preferred over NSAIDs in a patient with chronic kidney disease? — Colchicine has less renal prostaglandin inhibition; NSAIDs risk worsening renal function.
What lifestyle advice reduces recurrent gout attacks in a tropical setting? — Increase water intake, avoid high‑purine foods, limit local alcoholic brews, maintain healthy weight.
When should urate‑lowering therapy be initiated in a patient with podagra? — After the acute attack resolves and serum uric acid remains >6 mg/dL.
Explain why a normal serum uric acid does not exclude gout in this patient. — Hyperuricemia can fall during an acute flare; crystal detection remains the gold standard.
What are the red‑flag features that mandate referral to a surgical team? — Suspected septic arthritis, rapidly expanding cellulitis, or development of tophaceous ulceration.
How would you manage a patient with podagra who cannot take NSAIDs due to peptic ulcer disease? — Use low‑dose colchicine or a short course of oral steroids.
